name: Arida
title: Son of Haman, the Agagite
summary: Aridata is known exclusively from the book of Esther, where he is listed among the ten sons of Haman – the man who conspired to exterminate the Jews in the Persian Empire under King Ahasuerus. After Queen Esther revealed her father's conspiracy and Haman himself was executed, a new royal decree was issued granting the Jews the right to self-defense. On the 13th of Adar, Aridata and his nine brothers fell as the Jews fought back against those who sought their harm. At Esther's further request, the bodies of the ten brothers were publicly hanged in Susa. In the narrative arc of the Purim story, the fate of Haman's sons represents a complete reversal: from planned genocide to deliverance and triumph for the Jewish community.

keyEvents.title: Haman's Exaltation and the Family in Power
keyEvents.description: Haman, the father of Aridata, was promoted to the highest position among the king's officials. This gave the entire family, including Aridata, a privileged status in the Persian Empire.

keyEvents.title: Haman's Plan to Destroy the Jews
keyEvents.description: Driven by hatred toward Mordecai, Haman devised a plan to destroy all the Jews throughout the Persian Empire—a plan that directly involved the fate of his own family.

keyEvents.title: Esther's Intercession for Her People
keyEvents.description: Queen Esther revealed Haman's evil plot to King Ahasuerus and pleaded for the salvation of the Jewish people, marking the turning point for Haman's family.

keyEvents.title: Haman's Execution
keyEvents.description: Haman was hanged on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai. His downfall marked the beginning of the end for his entire household.

keyEvents.title: The Killing of Haman's Sons, Including Aridata
keyEvents.description: Aridata was killed along with his nine brothers when the Jews defended themselves against their enemies on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar, in accordance with the king's decree.

keyEvents.title: Haman's Sons Hanged on Gallows
keyEvents.description: At Esther's request, King Ahasuerus ordered that the bodies of Haman's ten sons, including Aridata, be hanged on gallows as a public sign of victory over the enemies of the Jews.

versions.summary: Aridata was one of the ten sons of Haman, the Agagite, who was an enemy of the Jewish people in Persia. He was killed along with his brothers when the Jews defended themselves against their enemies following King Ahasuerus' decree. His death marked God's protection of His people during the exile.
versions.title: Son of Haman
versions.reason: [minor] The title is correct but could be made slightly more descriptive to provide context.; [major] The events in the book of Esther are usually dated to around 480–470 BC (during the reign of Xerxes I / Ahasuerus). '400s BC' is technically possible but imprecise. More accurate would be 'around 480 BC' or 'around the 5th century BC'; [minor] The phrase 'during the exile' is somewhat misleading. The book of Esther takes place in the Persian diaspora after Babylon's fall, not during the exile itself in the strict sense. The Jews had already been permitted to return, but many remained in Persia. The wording should be adjusted.; [minor] There is no biblical evidence that Aridata was a 'warrior'. He was the son of a high-ranking official. The role 'son of Haman' is more precise. He is mentioned only as one of Haman's sons who were killed.; [major] Aridata is included in his own sibling list. He should be removed from there. In addition, the brother 'Dalephon' is missing – the list has 'Dalphon', which may be an acceptable variant, but most importantly, Aridata himself must be removed from the siblings list. The ten sons are: Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha, Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha, Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai, and Vaeshtatha. 'Aridai' is missing from the list.; [minor] The description says 'Haman's father' but means 'Aridata's father' (i.e., Haman). The phrasing 'Haman's father was exalted' is incorrect – it is Haman himself who was exalted. The text should say 'Haman was exalted' or 'Aridata's father, Haman, was exalted'.; [minor] Aridata had nine brothers, and the description says 'nine brothers', which is correct. However, it is worth noting that they were killed first, and then hanged (the next event). The wording is acceptable.; [major] Footnotes are missing. Interesting aspects include: the meaning of the name, Haman's identity as an Agagite, the festival of Purim as a result, and Persian historical context.

versions.summary: Aridata was one of the ten sons of Haman, the Agagite, who was an enemy of the Jewish people in the Persian Empire. He was killed along with his brothers when the Jews defended themselves against their enemies following King Ahasuerus' decree. Afterwards, he and his brothers were hanged on gallows at Esther's request. Aridata's death is part of the Purim story and illustrates God's protection of His people in the Persian diaspora.

versions.summary: Aridata is mentioned in the book of Esther as one of Haman's ten sons. Haman, who held the title Agagite, was the foremost opponent of the Jewish people during King Ahasuerus' reign in the Persian Empire. When the king's new decree gave the Jews the right to defend themselves against their enemies, Aridata was killed along with all his brothers on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar. At Esther's request, the bodies of the ten brothers were hung on gallows as a public testimony to this turning point. The fate of Aridata and his brothers forms part of the dramatic climax of the Purim story and points to how threats against God's people were turned into victory.

footnotes.text: The name Aridata is likely of Persian origin. Some scholars connect it to the Old Iranian 'Aryadata', which may mean 'given by the Arya/noble people'. This reflects that Haman's family had Persian names, even though he is described as an 'Agagite'.

The designation 'Agagite' for Haman has been interpreted as a possible connection to Agag, king of the Amalekites who was defeated by Saul (1 Sam 15). This places the conflict between Haman and Mordecai (of the tribe of Benjamin) within a broader theological framework of the ancient enmity between Israel and Amalek.

The festival of Purim, celebrated by Jews on the 14th and 15th of Adar, was instituted to commemorate deliverance from Haman's plot. The killing of Haman's ten sons, including Aridata, is a central part of the Purim story and is read aloud from the Scroll of Esther (Megillat Ester) during the celebration.

The Persian Empire under Ahasuerus (usually identified with Xerxes I, c. 486–465 BC) was a vast empire stretching from India to Ethiopia. Archaeological finds from Susa (biblical Shushan), including palace ruins, confirm the historical setting of the Book of Esther.

According to rabbinic tradition (Megilla 16a), the names of Haman's ten sons were written in a special column in the Scroll of Esther, with extra spaces between them, to symbolize that they were hanged on a long gallows, one below the other.

In Persian tradition, it was common to hang the bodies of executed enemies as a deterrent and symbolic gesture. The hanging of Haman's sons served both as just retribution and as a public demonstration of the shift in power to the advantage of the Jews.
